# Session 10: Reproducibility, Limits & Ethics

## 📋 Agenda

For three days you have checked an LLM's output against a gold standard. Today: **how to report the result honestly.**

- **Reproducibility** — pin · log · `temperature=0` + seed · **freeze**
- **Limits** — hallucination, data contamination, stochasticity
- **Ethics** — privacy, authorship, and what a licence actually asks of you
- **The reporting checklist** — the six sections you will hand in

::: {.callout-note}
This is the switch from tutorial mode to **project mode**. Everything after this session is your own study.
:::

## 🎯 Learning Objectives {.smaller}

By the end of this session, you will be able to:

- Name the four practices that make an LLM result reproducible, and apply them to your own run.
- Explain why `temperature=0` is **not sufficient**, and what freezing your predictions adds.
- Say which of hallucination, contamination and stochasticity your own track is exposed to.
- Apply the five-section reporting checklist — including saying what your numbers do **not** show.

# Reproducibility

## The problem, stated plainly

You run your prompt and get F1 = 0.62. Tomorrow you run the same prompt and get **0.58**.

. . .

Which number goes in the report?

. . .

Neither, until you can say *why they differ*. A result you cannot reproduce is not yet a finding.

## Four practices

| | Practice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Pin the model + version** | `gemini-3.1-flash-lite` ≠ `gemini-2.5-flash`. Models are silently retired and replaced. |
| 2 | **Log the prompt** | as a *file*, versioned — not a string you overwrote |
| 3 | **`temperature=0` + a fixed seed** | removes the sampling randomness you control |
| 4 | **Save the predictions to a file** | removes the variation you *cannot* control |

## Why `temperature=0` is not enough

`temperature=0` says *"always take the most likely next token."* That should be deterministic.

. . .

It mostly is. But you are calling a **hosted service**:

- the model behind the name can be updated underneath you
- batching and hardware differences perturb floating-point arithmetic
- the endpoint may silently fall back to another region

. . .

So a hosted LLM is only ***best-effort* reproducible**. You cannot fix this; it is a property of using a hosted service.

## The solution: run once, then save the output

```{.python}
predictions = run_prompt(PROMPT, gold)          # ← the ONE run
save_predictions(predictions, "outputs/cefr_groupA_predictions.json")
```

From then on, every number comes out of **that file**:

```{.python}
pred_final = load_predictions("outputs/cefr_groupA_predictions.json")
evaluate(gold, pred_final, ordered=True)        # the same answer every time
```

. . .

You did this on **Day 2** — you loaded a frozen predictions file we made for you, which is why the whole class got identical numbers. Now you make your own.

## What freezing gives you

- **A stable number** — your reported F1 does not change while you write the report.
- **No quota use** — re-running the analysis makes no further model calls.
- **Recomputable by others** — anyone, including whoever grades it, can recompute your numbers *from exactly the outputs you saw*.

::: {.callout-important}
The third point is the important one. "Reproducible" does not mean *you* can get the number again. It means **someone else can.**
:::

# LLM limitations

## Three failure modes

**Hallucination** — the model produces fluent output that is incorrect.

**Data contamination** — the model may have seen your test data in training.

**Stochasticity** — the same input gives different outputs.

. . .

For a *classification* task like yours, the first is limited because the label set is closed, and you have just handled the third. **The second is the one that affects your claims.**

## Contamination: why it matters here

Every track you can pick uses a **published** dataset.

- CEFR-SP is on GitHub. RAAMove is on GitHub. CaRS-50 is on Mendeley. AutoErrorAnalyzer is on OSF.
- These were all published *before* the model's training cutoff.

. . .

So when the model labels a sentence correctly, there are two explanations:

1. it understands the construct
2. **it has seen this sentence with this label before**

. . .

You cannot distinguish these two explanations from your F1 alone. State this in your report.

## What you can honestly claim

::: {.callout-warning}
## Not claimable
"Gemini can annotate CEFR level with F1 = 0.62."
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Claimable
"On 42 items from CEFR-SP, with this prompt and this model version, macro-F1 was 0.62. The corpus is public and predates the model's training cutoff, so contamination cannot be ruled out."
:::

The second sentence is *easier to defend* and *more useful to a reader*.

# Ethics

## Three things worth ten minutes

**Privacy.** Learner data is people's writing. ICNALE is licensed for research use only and may not be redistributed — which is why it is excluded from git and from your submission bundle by name.

**Authorship.** The model is a tool, not a co-author. But *what it did* belongs in your methods: which model, which prompt, which parameters.

**Licences have practical consequences.** CEFR-SP is CC BY-**SA**: anything you redistribute from it inherits share-alike. That is why the template's data folder carries its own `LICENSE` file.

## A limitation of your own study

You are about to measure a model against a gold standard built by **two of you**, on **40 items**, in **25 minutes**.

. . .

That is a small gold standard, built quickly, and it contains errors.

. . .

So is most of the published literature. The difference between good and bad work here is not the size of the gold set — it is **whether you say what it was.**

# The reporting checklist

## Six sections

| | Section | The thing that makes it good |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Intro | why this topic matters |
| 2 | Methodology | sampling · scheme & gold · split — and **what adjudication changed** |
| 3 | Prompt iterations | a *reason* per round, not just an F1 |
| 4 | Evaluation | which class did worst, and what it got confused with |
| 5 | Error analysis | model error or unclear scheme — with evidence |
| 6 | Limitations | ≥2 that apply to **your** run |

Two pages, written **individually**. One study per group, one report per person.

## How the report is graded

::: {.callout-important}
## Your F1 is not graded
A careful study reporting **F1 = 0.31** with a clear account of *why* scores higher than a sloppy one reporting **0.82**.
:::

. . .

The reason is that a number you cannot explain is not a finding, and that distinction is what the whole course is about.

. . .

So pick the track that will teach you something, not the one that will produce a high score. `cars50` is the hardest track *because* its own annotators only reached κ ≈ 0.43, which makes it the best track for showing that you can distinguish "the model is wrong" from "the scheme is unclear".
